input.brief:
CREATIVE BRIEF: Livetrust Financial (Kevin Martinez). 20 Reels scripts. Delivery date 2026-10-13.

INTERPRETATION (stated explicitly)
1. The client profile's main objective talks about Instagram carousels, but today's job asks for Reels. We treat today's deliverable as 20 spoken-English Reels scripts (35–60 s each) for Instagram Reels and TikTok. Brand voice, compliance rules and the disclaimer are the same as for carousels.
2. "Based on recent TikTok/Instagram research" means two things. First, format and hook patterns that are working now in the business-financing, SBA and small-business niche (structure, pacing, retention devices, on-screen text style). Second, the questions and objections real audiences are raising. It does NOT mean copying creators, using trending audio we can't license, or importing unverified claims from videos. Every financial fact still needs a verified, preferably official, source.
3. Yesterday's registry (KM-20261012-R01 to R20, all "propuesto") is the do-not-repeat list. Today's 20 must be new angles. We can link to yesterday's topics, but we can't restate them.
4. Success goals: discovery, retention, shares and qualified DM conversations. We never promise or imply virality, reach or view counts. Views are not leads. Each script names which goal it mainly serves.
5. IDs: KM-20261013-R01 to KM-20261013-R20.

OBJECTIVE
Position Kevin as a clear, trustworthy business-financing educator. Prompt qualified conversations by DM ("Have questions about financing your business? Send us a DM.") from US buyers of franchises or existing businesses and from owners looking for growth or working-capital funding.

MIX (5 per pillar, new angles only; final selection by AG-003)
- SBA loans explained. Not covered yesterday: the guaranty and what it means for the lender vs. you, the SBA 504 structure in depth (CDC + bank + borrower), SBA Express vs. standard 7(a), collateral expectations, why SBA fees and rates are capped or regulated (figures only if verified and labeled "as of Oct 2026, subject to change"), a realistic look at what happens after you apply (stages, NO timelines promised), and a 7(a) maximum loan amount explainer if verified.
- Buying a franchise. Not covered: royalties and ad fund hitting cash flow, resale franchise vs. new unit, multi-unit expectations, what to ask the franchisor before you talk to a lender, conversion franchise basics, and the FDD Item 20 / talking to existing franchisees (no Item 7 or Item 19 repeats).
- Buying an existing business. Not covered: SDE vs. EBITDA in plain English, due diligence basics, a partner buyout as an acquisition, what happens to existing debt and leases, earn-outs vs. seller notes (avoid repeating the seller-note explainer), and the questions to ask a seller before making an offer.
- Getting loan ready. Not covered: writing a use-of-funds statement (deeper than the R19 mention), what a lender-ready business plan contains, interim financials and a debt schedule, the personal financial picture lenders review (no credit repair), and how to prepare for a first lender conversation.
- Format variety: no more than 4 of any single format. Use these formats: myth_vs_reality, scenario (clearly hypothetical, round numbers), comparison, objection, question, checklist, practical_explainer, direct_statement, and also "storytime-style hypothetical" or a "3 questions to ask" format if research supports it.

SCRIPT SPEC (every script)
ID | pillar | format | primary goal | hook (spoken, 0–3 s, plus on-screen text) | beat-by-beat with timestamps and on-screen text | retention device | estimated words and duration (about 85–145 words at 145–150 wpm, 35–60 s) | caption ending with the exact disclaimer | 3–5 hashtags | sources used (real URLs from AG-002 only) | risk note.
- Write numbers the way they're spoken ("seven-A", "five-oh-four"). Explain jargon on first use.
- CTA: Instagram DM only. No links, lead magnets, "comment X" automations or services that aren't in the knowledge base.
- Deal size: the provisional ~USD 300,000 figure should be avoided by default. If a script uses it, it must say whether it means financing requested, annual revenue or purchase price, and must label that interpretation as provisional and pending Kevin's confirmation.

DESIGNER NOTES (AG-005: no structured slot in this handoff, so they're included here for the package)
- Placeholder brand: #0B2545 / #13315C / #E0A526 / #F4F6F8, Inter.
- 9:16 Reels with burned-in captions inside the safe zones (clear of the top 250 px and bottom 350 px UI areas).
- Design for talking head plus text overlays and simple motion graphics. No red alarm colors, no money-rain or hype stock imagery, no SBA or government logos or seals.
- Suggest a b-roll or graphic idea per beat.

RISKS FLAGGED BEFORE WORK STARTS
1. Compliance: no guarantees of approval, rates, terms or timelines ("fast approval", "get funded in X days" are banned). Not personalized advice. No implied SBA or government endorsement, and no SBA logos. The disclaimer goes verbatim at the end of every caption.
2. Accuracy: all program figures (7(a) max, 504 structure percentages, guaranty percentages, fees, equity injection rules, SOP 50 10 8.x status) must come from SBA.gov, eCFR or the current SOP, and must be labeled "as of Oct 2026, subject to change". Yesterday's notes flagged that form versions and post-2026 citizenship and eligibility changes are only partially verified. Re-verify, and don't build on yesterday's unverified items.
3. Client facts: Kevin's credentials, experience, deal history, lender partners, geography, handle and website are all unknown. Don't state or imply any of them (no "I've closed 100 deals", no "our lender partners").
4. Scope: business financing only. No personal finance, credit repair, crypto or get-rich content.
5. Platform claims: no promises of virality or reach. Trend observations must be attributed to real sources or labeled as qualitative observation. No invented engagement statistics.
6. Repetition: AG-003 checks for overlap against yesterday's 20 entries.

OUTPUT
Everything is a proposal for the human operator to approve. Nothing is published, posted or sent.

assignments.AG-002:
Research Specialist. Two tracks, real sources only, and never fabricate a URL, statistic or creator example.

(A) Platform research (recent TikTok and Instagram Reels, business financing / SBA / franchise / buy-a-business niche):
- Find 8–12 current hook and format patterns, with typical length, pacing, on-screen text style and retention devices.
- Find the recurring audience questions and objections (comments, FAQs).
- For each pattern give the source (link, or a description of where you observed it plus the date), and label it as an observed pattern, not a guaranteed result.
- If your tools can't access TikTok or Instagram directly, say so plainly and use accessible secondary sources (platform creator guidance, reputable marketing publications). Never present guesses as data. No engagement or virality statistics unless sourced.

(B) Fact verification for the candidate topics in the brief:
- SBA 7(a) maximum loan amount and guaranty percentages.
- SBA Express basics.
- 504 structure (CDC / bank / borrower shares, eligible uses).
- Collateral expectations.
- Guaranty fee and rate caps.
- The SOP 50 10 currently in effect as of Oct 2026 (confirm 8.1 status and any 2026 changes, including citizenship/eligibility changes).
- FDD Item 20 and other FDD items as used.
- SDE vs. EBITDA definitions.
- Earn-out basics.
Prefer SBA.gov, eCFR (13 CFR 120), the SOP text and FTC (Franchise Rule). Use reputable law-firm or bank sources only as secondary, and label them that way.

Deliver:
- A fact table with these columns: claim | status (verified / partially verified / unverified) | source URL | date accessed | suggested hedge wording ('as of Oct 2026, subject to change').
- A 'do not use' list.
- Mark explicitly anything you could not verify. Do not research or state anything about Kevin's credentials, partners or geography.
assignments.AG-003:
Content Strategist. Select 20 Reel topics (KM-20261013-R01 to R20), 5 per pillar: SBA loans explained, Buying a franchise, Buying an existing business, Getting loan ready.

Overlap check:
- Check every topic against the 20 registry entries from KM-20261012.
- Banned repeats: SBA lends the money myth; what is 7(a); 7(a) vs. 504 comparison; SBA paperwork objection; working-capital Q&A; franchise lender checklist; FDD Item 7 / Item 19; big brand ≠ funding; ramp-up working-capital scenario; 3 questions before a franchise; seller note explainer; business vs. buyer reality check; DSCR walkthrough; asking price vs. lender number; 3 numbers before buying; document checklist; equity injection explainer; credit vs. projections objection; 5 mistakes; lender fit.
- A new angle on a related subject is fine if the angle is clearly different. Note the related registry ID and the difference.

Use AG-002's research to:
- match topics to the questions real audiences are asking;
- pick formats, with no more than 4 of any one format and at least 7 different formats overall.

For each topic give:
- pillar, format, primary goal (discovery / retention / shares / DM conversation), hook angle and retention device;
- the AG-002 facts it depends on;
- any risk.

At least 5 topics should be built to start qualified DM conversations (intent-qualifying, e.g. 'planning to buy within 12 months') without hard-selling.

Drop or swap any topic whose key fact AG-002 marks unverified. Avoid the provisional ~$300k figure unless the topic truly needs it. If it's used, specify which interpretation and label it provisional.
assignments.AG-006:
Quality Supervisor. Review all 20 scripts before the package goes to the human operator. Check each script and report PASS, FIX (with a specific correction) or BLOCK.

1. Completeness: 20 scripts, IDs KM-20261013-R01 to R20, all required fields present.
2. Duration: 35–60 s, and the word count matches the duration at 145–150 wpm.
3. Accuracy: every figure and program claim traces to an AG-002 verified source, carries 'as of Oct 2026, subject to change' style hedging, and doesn't rely on anything unverified or on 'do not use' items. No fabricated sources or statistics.
4. Compliance: no guarantees of approval, rates, terms or timelines; no personalized advice; no SBA or government endorsement or logos; the disclaimer is verbatim at the end of every caption.
5. Client facts: nothing invented about Kevin (credentials, experience, partners, geography, handle, website). The ~$300k figure is absent, or specified and labeled provisional.
6. Scope: business financing only.
7. CTA: Instagram DM only; no links, lead magnets or automations.
8. Repetition: no topic or hook duplicates the KM-20261012 registry; formats are varied (no more than 4 of any one format).
9. Brand voice: plain English, jargon explained, no hype, no virality or reach promises.
10. Designer notes: placeholder palette and Inter, safe zones, no hype imagery.

Finish with:
- an overall verdict;
- a list of items the operator must re-verify on SBA.gov before publishing;
- a reminder that nothing is published or sent and that the package is for operator approval only.

## Overview
The SBA 7(a) loan is the most popular type of loan backed by the U.S. Small Business Administration, and you can use an SBA loan to acquire a business, and in fact, that's the SBA 7(a) loan's primary use case.

## Key Features
- **Loan Amount**: Borrowers can secure a maximum of $5 million under this loan program
- **Loan Terms**: The term-lengths of an SBA 7(a) loan extend up to 10 years for a business acquisition or working capital, and up to 25 years if the purchase includes real estate
- **Coverage**: This helps simplify the acquisition process by bundling the purchase price, working capital and even real estate costs into a single loan package, which often requires a lower down payment than traditional financing

## Requirements for Buyers
Buyers must be a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident, have a strong personal credit history with a FICO score of around 680 or higher, have relevant industry experience or a qualified partner, and demonstrate an ability to repay the loan with either cash flow, fixed assets, or cash reserves.

## Equity Contribution
If a completely new owner is acquiring a business, the SBA will ask that the buyer make a 10% equity injection.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about SBA loans, down payments, and equity injection for buying a business:

## Key SBA Down Payment Requirements

The SBA requires at least a 10% down payment on loans if the loan proceeds are being used to cover a change of ownership. This is called the "Down Payment (Equity Injection)" — the borrower's contribution to total project costs, not just the purchase price.

## Important Nuance: You Don't Need All Cash

The 10% doesn't have to come entirely from your own savings—up to half of it can come from a seller's note, with a minimum of 5% coming directly from you. Seller financing can typically count toward up to half of the required 10% equity injection, provided the seller note is on full standby — no principal or interest payments — for at least the first 24 months of the 7(a) loan.

## Total Project Cost Matters

The SBA's 10% equity injection requirement is based on total project cost, not the purchase price of the business, which includes the purchase price plus working capital, franchise fees, professional fees, and loan closing costs.

## Higher Requirements Possible

Although a 10% down payment is common, some lenders may require higher equity injections (up to 30% of the loan amount) for companies with weak cash flow or low-value collateral.

WHAT I FOUND
- 29 direct TikTok video URLs, all exactly as they appeared in search results. I built or edited none of them.

I also left out off-topic or out-of-scope results: PPP "grant" link videos, business-credit "$100K in 90 days" hype, the T-Mobile "$299 franchise" pitch, stock-backed loans, home loans and TikTok Shop.

WHAT I CANNOT VERIFY (APPLIES TO ALL REFERENCES)
- Post dates. Many results look older than 2026. Only two captions mention a year: R17 says "2026" and R23 says "2025". The search tool does not return recent-only results, so I can't confirm this set reflects what is working now.
- Views, likes, shares, comments, spoken hooks, transcripts, length, pacing and on-screen text. None of these were in the results.
- Whether a creator is credentialed or a licensed lender. Several are sellers of courses or services.
- Whether a caption's claims are accurate. Some summaries from the search tool attributed claims to TikTok creators that did not appear in any listed caption (for example "7(a) up to $5M with 10% down, the business pays it back, not you", and "only 3 documents to apply"). I did not tie these to any URL. Treat them as unverified, and do not use them.

PATTERNS ACROSS CAPTIONS (my qualitative reading, not data, not a promise of results)
1. Contrarian "reality check" opener ("It's surprisingly tough…", "Reality check: It's about the business, NOT you").
2. Number-led "X ways / X steps" listicles ("2 ways…", "3 ways…", "3 easy steps", "3 Franchises You Need To Avoid").
3. Direct-question hooks ("What is the SBA…?", "Are you thinking about registering an LLC…?", "What Is a Royalty?").
4. "Crash course" explainers of a single term (guaranty fee, royalty, due diligence).
5. Reply-to-comment videos ("Replying to @…"). This supports an objection or question format.
6. Comparisons against conventional loans (down payment). The specific percentages in these captions are not verified.
7. Low-money-down and seller-financing angles. These draw high interest but are the riskiest for compliance.
8. Comment- or DM-keyword CTAs ("DM 'Franchise'", "Dm me PROFIT", "Comment 'T-Mobile'"). The brief bans comment automations. A plain DM invitation is the only approved CTA.

QUESTIONS THESE SUGGEST AUDIENCES ARE ASKING (inferred from caption topics, not from comments I read)
- How much down payment do I need?
- Can seller financing replace the bank?
- What does the guaranty fee cost?
- Why are lenders selective about small acquisition loans?
- What does a franchise royalty do to my income?
- Do I need an LLC before I apply?
- What does due diligence involve?
- What does a franchise owner actually earn?

DO NOT EMULATE
- "No money down" and "buy a business for $0" framing.
- "Get approved" or "funded fast" language.
- Celebrity franchise-profit claims (R29).
- The comment-keyword CTAs above.
- Implying SBA backing means the government is the lender.
- Inaccurate FDD descriptions (R24 calls it "Federal Disclosure Documents … filed … for each state". The FTC Franchise Rule term is Franchise Disclosure Document. Track B should confirm the correct terms and filing facts before any script uses them).

topics.topic: [Pillar: SBA loans explained] Myth vs. reality: 'The SBA guarantee protects me if my business fails.' In fact, the guaranty protects the lender, and you still owe the full loan. | Hook angle: 'The SBA guarantee is not there for you. Here's who it protects.' On-screen: 'SBA guaranty = protection for…?' | Retention device: the answer is held back until about 8 s, then a twist on the personal guaranty | Risk: must not sound like fear-mongering. Use a calm tone, give no default statistics, and avoid any guaranty percentage unless AG-002 verifies it and labels it 'as of Oct 2026, subject to change'.
topics.audience: First-time SBA borrowers (franchise buyers, acquisition buyers, growth owners) who see 'government-backed' and assume it lowers their personal risk
topics.problem: Viewers misread 'government-guaranteed' as protection for the borrower. That misunderstanding shapes how they weigh personal risk before they borrow.
claims_to_verify: The SBA 7(a) guaranty covers a portion of the loan for the lender in case of borrower default, and does not reduce the borrower's repayment obligation (SBA.gov / 13 CFR 120)
Current SBA 7(a) guaranty percentages by loan size (e.g. 85% / 75% thresholds), only if they will be shown, with the source and 'as of Oct 2026'
Personal guaranty requirement: owners of 20% or more generally must personally guarantee SBA 7(a) loans (SOP 50 10 8.x section, current version)

**Equity Injection Requirements:**
Under SOP 50 10 8, the minimum equity injection is 10% for both startup businesses and complete changes of ownership. Seller standby notes, other standby debt, and money from passive investors are all "limited" sources now, and combined they can cover no more than half of the injection.

Buyer rebates tied to post-close performance are expressly allowed (seller earnouts remain prohibited, and rebate proceeds must pay down principal).

**Business Valuation and Closing Costs:**
Your QoE and valuation costs count toward the injection.

I found relevant information about SBA SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) collateral requirements. Based on the search results:

The lender must collateralize the loan to the maximum extent possible up to the loan amount. If fixed assets do not fully secure the loan, the lender must take available equity in the personal real estate of the principals as collateral.

Regarding the 25% equity threshold for personal residences, the SBA does not require a lender to collateralize a loan with a personal residence to meet the "fully secured" definition when the equity in the residence is less than 25% of the property's fair market value.

Additionally, the SBA has repeatedly said publicly and in testimony before committee that it will not decline a borrower for a lack of collateral. This indicates that while lenders must pursue collateral to the maximum extent possible, inadequate collateral alone should not result in loan denial.

These provisions appear to be part of the SBA's 7(a) lending program guidelines, which require lenders to balance thorough collateralization with practical lending standards that don't penalize borrowers solely on insufficient collateral availability.

## Collateral Requirements by Loan Size

The SBA does not require collateral on 7(a) Small or SBA Express loans of $50,000 or less.

For loans between $50,001 and $350,000, the lender must follow the written collateral policy it uses for similarly sized non-SBA commercial loans. SBA Express lenders may apply their own policy above $50,000 on loans up to $500,000.

SOP 50 10 8 requires collateral for all loans over $50,000, a tenfold reduction in the threshold from the prior version. Under SOP 50 10 7.1, collateral was required only for loans exceeding $500,000.

## Important Protection for Borrowers

Per SBA SOP 50 10 8, lenders cannot decline an otherwise-eligible loan solely because of insufficient collateral.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about SOP 50 10 8 business valuation requirements:

## Key Changes in Valuation Requirements

**Prior to SOP 50 10 8.1 (effective June 1, 2025):**

Under the prior SOP a lender could perform its own business valuation where the financed business value, net of real estate and equipment, was $250,000 or less. Additionally, an independent business valuation from a qualified source was required when the goodwill portion of the purchase price exceeds $250,000, or when the buyer and seller have a close relationship.

**New Requirements in SOP 50 10 8.1:**

Every change of ownership requires an independent Qualified Source valuation commissioned by and prepared for the lender. This represents a significant change—that exception does not appear anywhere in SOP 50 10 8.1.

## Qualified Source Requirements

The SOP names the qualifying credentials: Accredited Senior Appraiser (ASA), Certified Business Appraiser (CBA), Accredited in Business Valuation (ABV), Certified Valuation Analyst (CVA) and Business Certified Appraiser (BCA). Additionally, each must be "independent of the loan production function, not involved in the approval of the transaction, and must not have the appearance of a conflict of interest."

## Standard Structure (50-40-10)

A third-party lender must provide at least 50% of the financing, the CDC provides up to 40% of the financing through a 100% SBA-guaranteed debenture, and the applicant provides at least 10% of the financing.

## New Business and Special Purpose Property Requirements

If the borrower's company has less than two consecutive years of operating history or if the building or assets to be financed are considered "special purpose" (e.g., gas stations or some medical clinics), the borrower must increase their contribution by 5% for a total of 15%, and the CDC lends 5% less for a total of 35%-- in cases where the borrowers meet both of these conditions, they must increase to 20%, and the CDC lends 30%.

This means:
- **New business only** or **special purpose only**: 50% lender, 35% CDC, 15% borrower
- **Both new business AND special purpose**: 50% lender, 30% CDC, 20% borrower

## Owner-Occupied Requirements

Must occupy at least 51% of the property being financed.

## SBA Express Program

The SBA Express has a maximum loan amount of $500,000 and allows revolving lines of credit up to 10 years. SBA Express lenders have delegated authority to process, close, service, and liquidate the 7(a) loan without SBA review. The SBA can issue a loan number in as little as 36 hours.

## Standard 7(a) Program (for comparison)

Export Working Capital, which is part of the 7(a) program, has a maximum loan amount of $5 million. For Standard 7(a) loans, the loan amount ranges from $350,001 to $5 million.

## Debenture Maximum Amounts

The CDC portion can finance up to 40% of the project cost, with a maximum loan amount of $5.0 million. Certain eligible energy-efficient or manufacturing projects may qualify for up to $5.5 million.

More specifically, small manufacturers (NAICS 31–33) can access $5.5 million per project, with no aggregate cap — meaning manufacturers can have multiple 504 projects, while the standard maximum is $5 million per project for most businesses, which is also the total outstanding SBA-guaranteed exposure limit across both 504 and 7(a) programs combined for non-manufacturing businesses.

## Eligible Project Types

The maximum can increase to $5.5 million per qualifying project for small manufacturers under NAICS codes 31 through 33 with U.S. production facilities, projects reducing the operating company's energy consumption by at least 10%, and certain renewable-energy production or renewable-fuel projects.

## CDC as Nonprofit Organizations

The CDC portion of the loan is provided by a Certified Development Company (CDC), a nonprofit corporation that is certified and regulated by the Small Business Administration (SBA).

Based on the search results, here's what 16 CFR 436.5 requires for these three items:

**Item 6 - Other Fees:**
Item 6 requires disclosure of all other fees that the franchisee must pay to the franchisor or its affiliates, or that the franchisor or its affiliates impose or collect in whole or in part for a third party. This includes recurring or occasional fees associated with operating a franchise such as royalties, advertising fees, and transfer fees.

**Item 20 - Outlets and Franchisee Information:**
Item 20 requires disclosure in tabular form of the total number of franchised and company-owned outlets for each of the franchisor's last three fiscal years. Item 20 also lists current and recent former franchisees.

**Item 17 - Renewal, Termination, Transfer, and Dispute Resolution:**
Item 17 requires disclosure in tabular form of a table that cross-references each enumerated franchise relationship item with the applicable provision in the franchise or related agreement. This includes provisions dealing with termination, renewal, transfer/sale, and dispute resolution.

## Royalties Based on Gross Sales

I've performed the web search for you. Here are the key findings related to buying an existing business, with emphasis on asset vs. stock purchases, liabilities, and due diligence:

## Asset vs. Stock Purchase

There are two main types of business purchases: an asset purchase (where you buy the business's assets but not its legal entity) and a stock purchase (where you buy the company as-is, including any liabilities and contracts). SBA lenders usually prefer asset purchases due to reduced legal complications.

In an asset sale, you acquire the business's specific assets (equipment, inventory, trade names, customer relationships, and goodwill) and don't inherit the seller's liabilities, pending lawsuits, or historical obligations. By contrast, in a stock sale, you acquire the legal entity itself, including whatever liabilities aren't visible on the surface.

## Due Diligence

Due diligence involves asking questions about contracts, leases, existing cash flow, and inventory, and checking zoning and environmental rules. When stock purchases occur, lenders perform deeper due diligence to evaluate contingent liabilities, legal exposures, or off-balance-sheet risks.

## Stock Purchase Restrictions

The SBA permits 7(a) financing for stock purchases only when the buyer obtains 100% ownership of the business.

## Definition of Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE)

SDE is defined by IBBA as a business's earnings before income taxes, non-operating income and expenses, nonrecurring income and expenses, depreciation and amortization, interest, and one owner's entire compensation, including benefits and personal expenses the business pays on the owner's behalf.

**Personal Financial Statement Timing:**

## Delegated Authority and the Preferred Lender Program (PLP)

The SBA may grant delegated authority to lenders to process, close, service, and liquidate certain 7(a) loans without prior SBA review. The Preferred Lenders Program is designed to streamline procedures by delegating the final credit decision and most servicing and liquidation authority and responsibility to carefully selected PLP lenders, with PLP loan approvals subject only to a brief eligibility review and the assignment of a loan number by SBA.

## E-Tran and Loan Authorization

For loans processed using a Lender's delegated authority (PLP, PLP-EWCP, SBA Express, or Export Express), the Lender submits the loan guaranty request with the loan terms and conditions in E-Tran, and the SBA loan number will be issued in E-Tran signaling the loan is approved.

## Non-Delegated Loan Processing

For non-delegated loans processed through the LGPC, the Lender submits the loan guaranty request with the loan terms and conditions in E-Tran, and SBA will review the application and issue the SBA loan number if the loan is approved. The LGPC has two physical locations: Citrus Heights, CA, and Hazard, KY, and processes 7(a) loan guaranty applications for lenders who do not have deleg

sources.title: SBA lender resources: Types of 7(a) loans
sources.relevant_excerpt: Search snippets only, because WebFetch to sba.gov was blocked. Snippets said: SBA guarantees up to 85% of loans of $150,000 or less and up to 75% of loans above $150,000. SBA Express has a 50% guaranty and a $500,000 maximum, and allows revolving lines of credit for up to 10 years. Express lenders have delegated authority to process, close, service and liquidate. The 36-hour figure for issuing a loan number appeared in a snippet, but the source was not clearly confirmed.

sources.title: SBA lender resources: 7(a) terms, conditions and eligibility
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: uses include buying, refinancing or improving real estate; short- and long-term working capital; refinancing business debt; machinery and equipment; furniture, fixtures and supplies; and complete or partial changes of ownership. Maximum standard 7(a) loan is $5 million. SBA's maximum guaranteed exposure is $3.75 million.

sources.title: Small Business Administration 7(a) Loan Guaranty Program (CRS)
sources.relevant_excerpt: CRS overview of 7(a) guaranty percentages, loan limits and fees. Cited as a secondary confirmation of the 85%/75% guaranty and the $5 million maximum.

sources.title: Small Business Administration 504/CDC Loan Guaranty Program (CRS)
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: a third-party lender provides at least 50% of the financing, the CDC up to 40% through a 100% SBA-guaranteed debenture, and the applicant at least 10%. Applicants with less than two years of operations, or financing special-purpose property, add 5% (15% total). If both apply, the applicant puts in 20% and the CDC lends 30%.

sources.title: eCFR :: 13 CFR 120.520 -- Purchase of 7(a) loan guarantees
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: a lender may demand in writing that SBA honor its guarantee if the borrower has been in default on any installment for more than 60 calendar days (conditions apply). Snippet from the 13 CFR 120 Subpart E listing: 'SBA may utilize all legal means available, including offset and judicial remedies.'

sources.title: SBA SOP 50 10 8, Lender and Development Company Loan Programs (effective 6/1/2025)
sources.publisher: U.S. SBA (copy hosted by Partner ESI)
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippets: delegated lenders (PLP, SBA Express) submit the guaranty request in E-Tran, and the SBA loan number is issued in E-Tran; for non-delegated loans the LGPC reviews and issues the loan number if approved. On leases: the term, including renewal options exercisable solely by the operating company, must be at least equal to the loan term. This is version 8, not 8.1.

sources.title: SOP UPDATE: SBA Publishes SOP 50 10 8.1 with Technical Policy Updates
sources.relevant_excerpt: Search summary: SOP 50 10 8.1 was released August 14, 2026, reissued with technical updates September 25, 2026 (Information Notice 5000-882227), and is effective for loans receiving SBA loan numbers on or after October 1, 2026.

sources.title: Best Practices: Updated Collateral Rules for Standard 7(a) Loans in 50 10 8
sources.relevant_excerpt: Industry commentary on SOP 50 10 8 collateral rules: no collateral required at $50,000 or less; lender's own policy above that for smaller loans; the maximum-extent-possible rule and personal real estate rule for larger loans.

sources.title: Do SBA Loans Require Collateral? The Rules by Loan Size
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: SBA does not require collateral on 7(a) Small or SBA Express loans of $50,000 or less. From $50,001 to $350,000, the lender follows its written policy for similar non-SBA loans. Express lenders may use their own policy above $50,000 up to $500,000. Lenders cannot decline an otherwise-eligible loan solely for insufficient collateral.

sources.title: SOP 50 10 8.1: What Changes for SBA Business Acquisitions
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: under the prior SOP, a lender could do its own valuation when the business value (net of real estate and equipment) was $250,000 or less, unless there was a close relationship. Under 8.1, every change of ownership requires an independent Qualified Source valuation commissioned by and prepared for the lender.

sources.title: Best Practices: A Review of Equity Injection Requirements Under SOP 50 10 8
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: minimum 10% equity injection of total project costs for start-ups and complete changes of ownership. For partial changes of ownership, less than 10% is allowed if debt-to-worth is no greater than 9:1 before the change.

sources.title: SBA 7(a) Earnouts: The Rules and Seller-Note Alternatives
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: seller earnouts are prohibited because 7(a) acquisitions cannot use contingent or indeterminate price consideration. Buyer rebates tied to post-close performance are allowed.

sources.title: SBA Franchise Directory Reintroduced Effective June 1, 2025
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: the Directory was dropped under SOP 50 10 7 (August 2023) and reintroduced by SOP 50 10 8 (June 1, 2025). Brands that meet the FTC franchise definition must be listed for their franchisees to get SBA financing. A secondary snippet mentioned a June 30, 2026 documentation deadline.

sources.title: eCFR :: 16 CFR 436.5 -- Disclosure items
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: Item 6 covers all other fees paid to the franchisor or its affiliates, or collected for a third party (royalties, advertising fees, transfer fees). Item 17 is a table on renewal, termination, transfer and dispute resolution. Item 20 gives outlet tables for the last three fiscal years and lists current and recent former franchisees. Items 5 and 12 are in the same section.

sources.title: A Consumer's Guide to Buying a Franchise
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: 'You may have to pay the franchisor royalties based on a percentage of your weekly or monthly gross income... even if you are losing money.' The guide recommends talking to franchisees, but the exact quote was not retrieved.

sources.title: What Is the FDD Disclosure Period?
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: the FDD must be given no less than 14 calendar days before the franchisee signs a binding agreement or pays any fee. There is a separate 7-day review period for materially changed agreements.

sources.title: Conversion Franchise Law and Legal Definition
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: a conversion franchise is a franchise system in which already existing independent businesses are converted into franchises.

sources.title: What Is SDE Sellers Discretionary Earnings: A Deep Dive
sources.relevant_excerpt: Search summary attributed this definition to IBBA: earnings before income taxes, non-operating and nonrecurring items, depreciation and amortization, interest, and one owner's total compensation, including benefits and personal expenses. EBITDA keeps a market-rate manager salary as a cost. The IBBA original was not retrieved.

sources.title: Asset vs Stock Purchase
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: in an asset purchase you buy assets, not the legal entity, and generally do not inherit the seller's liabilities. In a stock purchase you acquire the entity, including its liabilities. Industry source, lower reliability.

sources.title: SBA Form 1919 (file named 3-2026)
sources.relevant_excerpt: Title suggests a March 2026 revision of SBA Form 1919, the 7(a) Borrower Information Form. A separate snippet says Form 1919 collects information on the applicant, its owners, the loan request, existing indebtedness and prior government financing. An SBA-hosted copy (caweb.sba.gov) is Revised 09/20.

sources.title: SBA Form 159: The Fee Disclosure Nobody Explains
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: SBA Form 159, the Fee Disclosure and Compensation Agreement, identifies every agent paid in connection with a 7(a) or 504 loan and what each was paid.

sources.title: Writing a Business Plan: Your Roadmap to Small Business Success
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: a traditional plan is comprehensive and commonly requested by lenders and investors. Sections may include executive summary, company description, market analysis and financial projections.

sources.title: SBA launches enhanced Lender Match platform (Archived news release 24-15)
sources.relevant_excerpt: SBA news release (March 4, 2024) about the enhanced Lender Match platform, which connects small businesses with participating SBA lenders.

sources.title: SBA 7(a) Personal Financial Statement Requirements (2026)
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: Form 413 is completed by each proprietor; general partner; managing member of an LLC; each owner of 20% or more; and any person providing a guaranty. Related snippet: under 8.1, PFS dating changes from 120 days to 90 days.

sources.title: SBA Lending Post-SOP 50 10 8: Understanding the Revitalized Credit Elsewhere Rule
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: this is not a return to the former Personal Resources Test, but SOP 50 10 8 re-emphasizes that the lender must ensure the applicant and owners of 20% or more do not have readily available funds. It lists reasonable exceptions (retirement, education, medical, 24-month capital needs, working capital).

sources.title: What Are the Occupancy Requirements of an SBA 504 Loan?
sources.relevant_excerpt: Search summary citing 13 CFR 120.131: at least 51% occupancy for existing buildings; 60% for new construction, with conditions. 504 proceeds cannot fund working capital or inventory.

sources.title: SBA 504 Loan Maximum Guidelines
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: the CDC portion may be up to 40% of project cost, with a maximum of $5.0 million ($5.5 million for qualifying manufacturing or energy projects). A CDC is a nonprofit certified and regulated by the SBA.

sources.title: Area Development Agreement vs Single-Unit Franchise
sources.relevant_excerpt: Snippet: missing development deadlines could lose you territorial exclusivity or the agreement itself. Consequences vary by franchisor, and development fees are often non-refundable.

sources.title: Understanding SBA 7(a) Loan Fees and Costs
sources.relevant_excerpt: Search summary: lenders may pass the upfront guaranty fee to the borrower, and borrowers may use loan proceeds to pay it. The first disbursement cannot be made solely or mainly for that purpose.

sources.title: SOP 50 10 8.1 for Lenders: The Four Acquisition Categories
sources.relevant_excerpt: Search summary: in a partial buyout, a selling owner who keeps any stake must give a full guaranty for at least two years. Industry interpretation of 8.1.

sources.title: Can You Get a $10M SBA Loan? New 2026 Rule Explained
sources.relevant_excerpt: Title only. It suggests a 2026 change to cumulative SBA loan limits (likely sector-specific). Not verified; flags that aggregate-limit statements may be out of date.

sources.title: Commercial Loan Service Center
sources.relevant_excerpt: Appeared in results about 7(a) loan processing and servicing centers. Snippet context: the LGPC processes guaranty applications for lenders without delegated authority.

claims.claim: The 7(a) guaranty protects the lender against default and does not reduce what the borrower owes
claims.correct_wording: The SBA guarantees part of a 7(a) loan to the lender. If the borrower defaults, the lender can ask the SBA to buy the guaranteed portion. The borrower still owes the full debt. (13 CFR 120.520.) Note: WebFetch was blocked. Based on eCFR search snippets only.

claims.claim: 7(a) guaranty percentages: 85% / 75%
claims.correct_wording: As of Oct 2026, the SBA guarantees up to 85% of 7(a) loans of $150,000 or less and up to 75% of loans over $150,000. SBA Express is 50%. Source: SBA.gov. These figures can change.

claims.claim: Owners of 20% or more must personally guarantee
claims.correct_wording: Owners of 20% or more generally must give a full, unlimited personal guaranty (13 CFR 120.160; SOP 50 10 8.1, effective for loan numbers issued on or after Oct 1, 2026). Lenders can ask other people to guarantee too. I did not get the exact SOP section number. Do not cite a section.

claims.claim: After paying the lender, the SBA may pursue recovery from the borrower and guarantors
claims.correct_wording: After a default, the remaining debt is still owed by the borrower and guarantors. The SBA 'may utilize all legal means available, including offset and judicial remedies' (13 CFR Part 120, Subpart E). SOP 50 57 was not checked. Do not cite it.

claims.claim: 504 structure: bank first lien, CDC second lien funded by an SBA-guaranteed debenture, borrower equity
claims.correct_wording: In a 504 loan, a third-party lender (usually a bank) finances part of the project with a first lien. A CDC finances part with a second lien, funded by a debenture that the SBA guarantees 100%. The borrower puts in equity.

claims.claim: Typical 50/40/10 split, with higher borrower contribution in some cases
claims.correct_wording: As of Oct 2026, the typical split is 50% lender, up to 40% CDC and at least 10% borrower. The borrower puts in 15% if the business has less than two years of operating history or the property is special-purpose. If both apply, the borrower puts in 20%. Source: CRS R41184.

claims.claim: 504 eligible uses are fixed assets, not working capital
claims.correct_wording: 504 loans pay for long-term fixed assets, such as real estate and long-life equipment. Working capital and inventory are not eligible uses. Note: SBA.gov could not be opened. This is based on CDC and industry sources.

claims.claim: Owner-occupancy requirement
claims.correct_wording: The business must occupy at least 51% of an existing building, or at least 60% of a newly built one, with further occupancy steps over time (13 CFR 120.131, as cited by a CDC).

claims.claim: 504 maximum debenture
claims.correct_wording: If used: the CDC/SBA portion is generally capped at $5 million per project, or $5.5 million for qualifying manufacturing or energy projects (CDC source, not SBA.gov). Not confirmed on SBA.gov. I recommend leaving it out.

claims.claim: What a CDC is
claims.correct_wording: A Certified Development Company (CDC) is a nonprofit that the SBA certifies and regulates to deliver 504 loans. CDCs generally serve a defined local area, but that part was not confirmed in snippets.

claims.claim: SBA Express maximum loan amount
claims.correct_wording: As of Oct 2026, SBA Express loans go up to $500,000 (SBA.gov).

claims.claim: Express guaranty compared with standard 7(a)
claims.correct_wording: SBA Express carries a 50% guaranty. Standard 7(a) is up to 85% for loans of $150,000 or less and 75% above that. As of Oct 2026.

claims.claim: Under Express, the lender makes the credit decision and the SBA responds to the guaranty request
claims.correct_wording: SBA Express lenders have delegated authority. They decide on credit using their own procedures and then send the guaranty request to the SBA through E-Tran. Leave out the '36 hours' figure: it was only in a snippet, and it would describe the SBA issuing a loan number, not funding.

claims.claim: Express supports revolving lines of credit
claims.correct_wording: Yes. SBA Express can be used for revolving lines of credit, with terms up to 10 years (SBA.gov, as of Oct 2026).

claims.claim: Standard 7(a) maximum loan amount
claims.correct_wording: As of Oct 2026, the standard 7(a) maximum is $5 million (SBA.gov).

claims.claim: General 7(a) process: lender underwrites, then submits for a guaranty or uses delegated authority, and the SBA issues a loan number
claims.correct_wording: The lender underwrites the loan. Lenders with delegated authority (such as PLP or SBA Express) approve it themselves and send it through E-Tran, where the SBA assigns a loan number. For other lenders, the SBA's Loan Guaranty Processing Center reviews the request and issues the loan number if approved.

claims.claim: Common closing items
claims.correct_wording: If an agent or packager is paid, SBA Form 159 (Fee Disclosure and Compensation Agreement) is required. Change-of-ownership deals need an independent business valuation. Insurance and lien filings are standard, but I found no official snippet listing them, so present them as 'commonly'.

claims.claim: A commitment letter commonly lists conditions to be met before closing
claims.correct_wording: No source was retrieved. If used, phrase it as 'Lenders commonly list the conditions to meet before closing in a commitment letter.' This varies by lender.

claims.claim: The SBA does not decline a loan solely because of inadequate collateral
claims.correct_wording: Under SOP 50 10 8, an otherwise-eligible loan is not to be declined solely because collateral is inadequate (industry sources; the exact SOP wording and section were not retrieved). Paraphrase it rather than quote it.

claims.claim: Collateral thresholds
claims.correct_wording: As of Oct 2026, no collateral is required for 7(a) loans of $50,000 or less. From $50,001 to $350,000 (up to $500,000 for SBA Express), lenders follow their own collateral policy for similar non-SBA loans. Above that, lenders must take available collateral to the maximum extent possible. Industry summaries of SOP 50 10 8; confirm in 8.1.

claims.claim: Liens on personal real estate (25% equity)
claims.correct_wording: If business assets don't fully secure a larger loan, lenders must take available equity in the owners' personal real estate. A personal residence is not required when the equity is less than 25% of its market value. This comes from a snippet with a mixed source. Confirm under 8.1 before using.

claims.claim: Do the rules differ for Express vs. standard 7(a)?
claims.correct_wording: Yes. SBA Express lenders may apply their own collateral policy for loans over $50,000 up to $500,000.

claims.claim: FDD Item 6 discloses other fees, including royalties and ad-fund contributions
claims.correct_wording: Under the FTC Franchise Rule (16 CFR 436.5(f)), Item 6 discloses other recurring or occasional fees paid to the franchisor or its affiliates, such as royalties and advertising fees.

claims.claim: Royalties are commonly a percentage of gross sales
claims.correct_wording: The FTC guide says: 'You may have to pay the franchisor royalties based on a percentage of your weekly or monthly gross income.' For ad funds, say only that the fee basis is shown in Item 6.

claims.claim: Lenders evaluate repayment from cash flow after expenses, including franchise fees
claims.correct_wording: No source was retrieved. Hedge it: 'Lenders generally look at whether cash flow after operating costs, including ongoing franchise fees, can cover loan payments.' Label all figures hypothetical.

claims.claim: Item 17 covers transfer; Item 6 may list transfer fees
claims.correct_wording: Item 17 summarizes renewal, termination, transfer and dispute-resolution terms. Item 6 may list a transfer fee (16 CFR 436.5).

claims.claim: Business valuation required above certain thresholds
claims.correct_wording: Under SOP 50 10 8.1 (effective Oct 1, 2026), every change of ownership reportedly needs an independent valuation from a qualified source, commissioned by the lender. The old $250,000 exception no longer applies. Industry source only, so confirm before airing. Do not describe it as 'above a threshold'.

claims.claim: Equity injection minimums for start-ups vs. changes of ownership
claims.correct_wording: Under SOP 50 10 8, the minimum is 10% of total project costs for start-ups (operating one year or less) and for complete changes of ownership. Whether 8.1 kept this is not confirmed, and 8.1 limits seller notes to at most half of the injection. Leave it out or attribute it to SOP 50 10 8.

claims.claim: Franchise eligibility through the SBA Franchise Directory
claims.correct_wording: Since SOP 50 10 8 (June 1, 2025), a brand that meets the FTC franchise definition must be on the SBA Franchise Directory for its franchisees to get SBA financing. As of Oct 2026, check the current Directory on SBA.gov.

claims.claim: Item 20 outlet data and franchisee contact lists
claims.correct_wording: Item 20 (16 CFR 436.5(t)) gives outlet data and lists current franchisees and franchisees who left the system recently. My understanding of the rule is 'during the last fiscal year', but snippets did not confirm that exact wording.

claims.claim: The FTC guide recommends talking to current and former franchisees
claims.correct_wording: The FTC guide encourages talking with current and former franchisees. I could not retrieve the exact wording, so paraphrase and do not use quotation marks.

claims.claim: Franchisee conversations help build realistic projections
claims.correct_wording: Advice to consider, not a rule: 'Talking with franchisees may help you build more realistic projections to share with a lender.'

claims.claim: FDD disclosures for development agreements (Items 5, 6, 12)
claims.correct_wording: Development fees are disclosed in Items 5 and 6, and territory rights in Item 12 (16 CFR 436.5). The development schedule itself is set out in the development agreement.

claims.claim: Missing the development schedule may cost territorial rights
claims.correct_wording: Depending on the agreement, missing development deadlines may mean losing territorial exclusivity or the development agreement itself.

claims.claim: Each new unit is evaluated on its own needs and on overall cash flow
claims.correct_wording: Hedge it: 'Lenders commonly look at each new unit's funding needs along with the borrower's overall cash flow and debt. Practices vary by lender.'

claims.claim: Affiliation and aggregate loan limits
claims.correct_wording: SBA.gov states a maximum guaranteed exposure of $3.75 million per borrower, including affiliates. There are reports of 2026 changes to cumulative limits that I could not verify. I recommend leaving this out.

claims.claim: Conversion franchise definition
claims.correct_wording: General definition: a conversion franchise is an existing independent business that joins a franchise system and adopts its brand and operating system.

claims.claim: The FDD still applies and the 14-day rule
claims.correct_wording: Under the FTC Franchise Rule (16 CFR 436), the franchisor generally must give the FDD at least 14 calendar days before the buyer signs a binding agreement or pays any fee. Exemptions exist.

claims.claim: Brand must be on the SBA Franchise Directory
claims.correct_wording: If the arrangement meets the FTC franchise definition, the brand must be on the SBA Franchise Directory to be eligible for SBA financing (since June 1, 2025). Check the current listing.

claims.claim: Lenders look at historical cash flow plus new franchise fees
claims.correct_wording: Hedge it: 'A lender would likely look at the business's past cash flow and how the new ongoing franchise fees would affect it.'

claims.claim: SDE definition
claims.correct_wording: SDE is generally defined as pre-tax earnings before interest, depreciation and amortization, plus one owner's total compensation and discretionary or one-time items. This definition is commonly credited to the IBBA, but I did not open the IBBA original.

claims.claim: EBITDA definition
claims.correct_wording: EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. In valuation it usually keeps a market-rate manager's salary as an expense.

claims.claim: SDE is used for smaller businesses and EBITDA for larger ones
claims.correct_wording: SDE is commonly used for smaller owner-run businesses and EBITDA for larger businesses with professional management. Do not give a dollar cutoff.

claims.claim: Lenders verify earnings against tax returns and add-backs need documentation
claims.correct_wording: Lenders generally check earnings against tax returns, and add-backs usually need documentation. SOP 50 10 8 requires lenders to check the seller information the valuator used against IRS transcripts.

claims.claim: Lenders review the seller's financial statements and tax returns
claims.correct_wording: In SBA change-of-ownership deals, lenders review the seller's financial information. Under SOP 50 10 8, they verify it against IRS tax transcripts. The exact document list under 8.1 was not retrieved.

claims.claim: Lease term vs. loan term
claims.correct_wording: Under SOP 50 10 8, the lease term, including renewal options the business alone can exercise, should be at least as long as the loan term. Confirm whether 8.1 changed this.

claims.claim: General diligence areas
claims.correct_wording: Common diligence areas include contracts, leases, cash flow, inventory, and zoning and environmental matters. The SBA.gov page itself could not be retrieved.

claims.claim: 7(a) can finance a partial change of ownership
claims.correct_wording: Yes. SBA.gov lists complete or partial changes of ownership as eligible 7(a) uses (as of Oct 2026).

claims.claim: Equity and guaranty rules for partial changes of ownership
claims.correct_wording: Under SOP 50 10 8, a partial buyout may need less than 10% equity if debt-to-worth is 9:1 or better before the change. Industry sources say a selling owner who keeps any stake must give a full guaranty for at least two years. Industry interpretation only, so confirm in SOP 8.1 or leave it out.

claims.claim: Business valuation thresholds
claims.correct_wording: Under 8.1, every change of ownership reportedly needs an independent qualified-source valuation, with no dollar threshold.

claims.claim: Asset vs. stock purchase and liabilities
claims.correct_wording: Generally, an asset buyer does not take on the seller's liabilities, while a stock buyer takes the whole company, liabilities included. Exceptions exist, so get legal advice.

claims.claim: Seller debts are paid off at closing to release liens
claims.correct_wording: Hedge it: 'Seller debts secured by business assets are commonly paid off at closing so the liens can be released.'

claims.claim: SOP lease term requirement
claims.correct_wording: Same as R12: under SOP 50 10 8, the lease term including the business's own renewal options should be at least the loan term. Confirm for 8.1.

claims.claim: Lease assignment needs landlord consent
claims.correct_wording: Hedge it: 'Many leases require the landlord's consent to assign the lease. Check the lease terms.'

claims.claim: Earn-outs in 7(a) change-of-ownership deals
claims.correct_wording: Under SOP 50 10 8/8.1, seller earn-outs are reportedly not allowed in 7(a) change-of-ownership deals, because the price can't be contingent. Buyer rebates are allowed. The exact SOP section was not retrieved.

claims.claim: Earn-out definition
claims.correct_wording: An earn-out is a contingent future payment to the seller that depends on how the business performs after closing.

claims.claim: Difference from a seller note
claims.correct_wording: A seller note has a fixed principal and set repayment terms. Refer to the earlier scripts for standby rules.

claims.claim: Proceeds must go to eligible uses listed in the authorization
claims.correct_wording: SBA loan proceeds must go to eligible uses. Form 1919 asks what the funds are for. That the authorization lists use of proceeds is standard, but no snippet confirmed it.

claims.claim: Eligible 7(a) uses
claims.correct_wording: As of Oct 2026, 7(a) loans can pay for working capital; equipment, furniture and fixtures; buying, building or improving real estate; changes of ownership; and refinancing business debt under certain conditions.

claims.claim: Sources and uses
claims.correct_wording: Hedge it: 'Lenders commonly use a sources-and-uses table, where the total sources (loan, equity, any seller financing) match the total uses.'

claims.claim: The guaranty fee can be financed
claims.correct_wording: Borrowers may generally pay the upfront guaranty fee from loan proceeds, with conditions on the first disbursement. Fees change each fiscal year.

claims.claim: SBA.gov business plan guidance
claims.correct_wording: SBA.gov describes a traditional business plan that may include an executive summary, company description, market analysis and financial projections, among other sections.

claims.claim: The SOP requires a business plan or projections
claims.correct_wording: Not verified. Leave it out, or say 'lenders commonly ask for projections'.

claims.claim: Projections should state their assumptions
claims.correct_wording: Phrase as advice: 'It's good practice to explain the assumptions behind your projections.'

claims.claim: Interim financial statements definition
claims.correct_wording: Interim financial statements are current year-to-date statements, usually a profit and loss statement and a balance sheet.

claims.claim: Form 1919 asks about existing business debt
claims.correct_wording: SBA Form 1919 collects information on existing indebtedness. A copy dated 3/2026 appears to be the current version, but confirm on SBA.gov.

claims.claim: How current interim financials must be
claims.correct_wording: Leave this out. (Only the personal financial statement dating rule turned up: 90 days under 8.1.)

claims.claim: A debt schedule is used to calculate total debt service
claims.correct_wording: Hedge it: 'Lenders commonly use a debt schedule to work out total debt payments (see DSCR).'

claims.claim: Form 413 required from certain owners
claims.correct_wording: SBA Form 413 (Personal Financial Statement) is completed by each proprietor, general partner, LLC managing member, owner of 20% or more, and any guarantor. Under 8.1, it must be dated within 90 days. I did not confirm the current form edition.

claims.claim: Personal guaranty for owners of 20% or more
claims.correct_wording: Same as R01: owners of 20% or more generally must give a full personal guaranty.

claims.claim: Personal resources / liquidity
claims.correct_wording: The old Personal Resources Test has not returned. But under SOP 50 10 8, lenders must still check that the applicant and owners of 20% or more don't have readily available funds that make the SBA loan unnecessary (the 'credit elsewhere' test), with reasonable exceptions.

claims.claim: Lenders consider owners' credit history
claims.correct_wording: Hedge it: 'Lenders generally review the owners' credit history.' Give no score figures.

claims.claim: General preparation guidance and Lender Match
claims.correct_wording: Lender Match is a free SBA tool that connects businesses with participating SBA lenders (enhanced in March 2024). It does not approve loans and is not an endorsement of any lender. I could not confirm its status as of Oct 2026. Label all characters hypothetical.

scripts.topic: [Getting loan ready] How to write a use-of-funds statement: a hypothetical line-by-line build where every line ties to a document, balanced against a sources column
scripts.audience: Any borrower preparing a request (franchise, acquisition, growth or working capital)
scripts.problem: Borrowers submit one lump-sum request without an itemized, documented breakdown, which invites back-and-forth and questions about whether the amount is justified.
scripts.amount_context: Hypothetical round figures only: build-out one hundred twenty thousand, equipment sixty thousand, working capital forty thousand, closing costs and fees ten thousand, total uses two hundred thirty thousand dollars. The ~USD 300,000 figure is not used.
scripts.hook: "I need about this much money" isn't a use of funds. Here's what one actually looks like.
scripts.script: "I need about this much money" isn't a use of funds. Here's what one actually looks like. Let's build a hypothetical one, line by line. Build-out: one hundred twenty thousand dollars, tied to a contractor quote. Equipment: sixty thousand, tied to a vendor quote. Working capital, meaning the cash that covers payroll and bills while revenue ramps up: forty thousand, tied to your projections. Closing costs and fees: ten thousand, tied to estimates from your lender. Total uses: two hundred thirty thousand. Now the other column, sources: the loan, your own cash, any seller financing. Lenders commonly lay this out side by side, and both columns have to match. On SBA seven-A loans, every dollar has to go to an eligible use, as of October twenty twenty-six, subject to change. Save this for when you build yours.

scripts.topic: [Getting loan ready] Checklist: six sections commonly found in a lender-ready business plan, with the assumptions behind projections as the section most plans skip
scripts.audience: Franchise start-up buyers and growth owners asked for a business plan; acquisition buyers asked for a transition plan
scripts.problem: Borrowers produce investor-style or template plans that lack the assumptions and management details a lender needs to judge repayment.
scripts.amount_context: No amounts used. The ~USD 300,000 figure is not referenced.
scripts.hook: A lender-ready business plan isn't a pitch deck.
scripts.script: A lender-ready business plan isn't a pitch deck. Here are six sections that commonly go into one. One: a business summary. What the business is, and what you're asking for. Two: management. Who runs it, and the experience they bring. Three: your market and your local competition. Four: operations. Location, staffing, how the day-to-day actually works. Five is the one most plans skip: the assumptions behind your projections. If you project a number, explain where it comes from. It's good practice, and it lets a lender follow your math. Six: the financial projections themselves, plus your use of funds. Lenders commonly ask for projections, so make them easy to check. This is a common structure, not an official template, and a plan alone doesn't mean approval. Save this before you start writing.
scripts.cta: Save this before you start writing.
scripts.recording_notes_es: Plano medio, energía firme pero tranquila. Marcar cada número con los dedos (uno a seis). Antes de 'Five is the one most plans skip', inclinarse un poco hacia la cámara y bajar apenas la voz, con una pausa de un segundo. Decir la aclaración de 'not an official template' en tono neutro, sin apurarla.

scripts.topic: [Getting loan ready] Question: what interim financials and a business debt schedule are, and why lenders want them on top of tax returns
scripts.audience: Existing owners seeking growth or working-capital funding, and buyers' or sellers' teams preparing acquisition packages
scripts.problem: Owners hand over only tax returns. Lenders then ask for current-year figures and a debt list, and outdated or missing numbers create delays and doubts.
scripts.amount_context: No amounts used. The ~USD 300,000 figure is not referenced.
scripts.hook: Your tax return shows last year. The lender also wants to see this year.
scripts.script: Your tax return shows last year. The lender also wants to see this year. So what are interim financials and a debt schedule? Interim financials are your current year-to-date statements, usually a profit and loss statement and a balance sheet. They show how the business is doing now, not just last year. A debt schedule is a list of every business debt: the lender, the balance, the monthly payment, and when it matures. The SBA seven-A borrower information form also asks about existing debt. Two documents, one purpose: a current picture of the business. Lenders commonly use that debt list to work out your total debt payments, which feeds into D-S-C-R, the debt service coverage ratio. How recent do your numbers need to be? Ask your lender. Save this so you're not caught with only tax returns.

scripts.topic: [Getting loan ready] Objection: 'It's a business loan, so why does the lender care about my personal finances?' The personal guaranty, the personal financial statement, the credit elsewhere test and the owners' credit history
scripts.audience: First-time borrowers (franchise and acquisition buyers) surprised by personal disclosure requests
scripts.problem: Borrowers resist or delay personal disclosures, or don't realize their personal liquidity and obligations affect how the lender sees the deal.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amounts used. Only the twenty percent ownership threshold is mentioned. The ~USD 300,000 figure is not referenced.
scripts.hook: "The business is borrowing, not me." Lenders see it differently.
scripts.script: "The business is borrowing, not me." Lenders see it differently. Here's why. One: the personal guaranty. On SBA loans, owners of twenty percent or more generally must personally guarantee the loan. If you're backing the loan, your finances are part of the picture. Two: the personal financial statement. For SBA loans, that's Form four-thirteen, completed by each owner of twenty percent or more, any guarantor, and certain others. It's a snapshot of what you own and what you owe. Three: what's called the credit elsewhere test. Lenders must check that you and those owners don't have readily available funds that make the SBA loan unnecessary, with reasonable exceptions. And lenders generally review the owners' credit history. It's not personal. It's how they see the whole deal. Rules as of October twenty twenty-six, subject to change. Share this with your business partner.
scripts.cta: Share this with your business partner.

scripts.script: Signing for three franchise units doesn't mean you get funding for three units. A multi-unit deal, often called a development agreement, is a schedule you promise to keep. scripts.hook: Already own a business? You might not need to start a franchise from scratch.
scripts.script: Already own a business? You might not need to start a franchise from scratch. It's called a conversion franchise. Here's how it works in three parts. One, what it is. The franchisor generally has to give you the disclosure document at least fourteen calendar days before you sign or pay any fee. There are some exemptions. Three, what a lender looks at. A lender would likely look at your past cash flow and how the new ongoing fees would affect it. For SBA financing, the brand generally needs to be on the SBA Franchise Directory. scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying an existing business] SDE vs. EBITDA in plain English: two ways to measure a business's earnings, who uses which, and why listings show both
scripts.audience: First-time acquisition buyers reading business-for-sale listings and broker packages
scripts.problem: Buyers compare listings that measure earnings differently and overestimate what is left to pay a loan and a manager.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amounts used. The provisional ~USD 300,000 figure is not mentioned.
scripts.hook: Two business listings both say "earnings." But one means SDE and the other means EBITDA, and those are not the same number.
scripts.script: Two business listings both say "earnings." But one means SDE and the other means EBITDA, and those are not the same number. SDE stands for seller's discretionary earnings. It's generally pre-tax earnings before interest, depreciation and amortization, plus one owner's full compensation and certain one-time or discretionary expenses. EBITDA means earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. In valuation, it usually keeps a market-rate manager's salary as an expense. So here's the key difference: the owner's paycheck. In SDE, it's added back. In EBITDA, it stays as a cost. In practice, SDE is commonly used for smaller, owner-run businesses, and EBITDA for larger ones with professional management. Either way, lenders generally check earnings against tax returns, and add-backs usually need documentation. These are general definitions, not valuation advice. Save this for the next listing you read.
scripts.cta: Save this for the next listing you read.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying an existing business] Due diligence basics: a 5-area checklist of what a buyer verifies about the target business before closing
scripts.audience: Acquisition buyers with an LOI or offer in progress

scripts.hook: Your offer got accepted. Now comes the part that's meant to protect you: due diligence.
scripts.script: Your offer got accepted. Now comes the part that's meant to protect you: due diligence. That's the verification work before closing. Here are five common areas to check. One: financials. Do the seller's statements match the tax returns? In SBA acquisitions, lenders generally verify the seller's numbers against IRS tax transcripts. Two: cash flow. Does the money actually come in the way the listing says? Three: the lease. Under SBA rules, as of October twenty twenty-six and subject to change, the lease term, including renewal options the business alone can use, generally needs to be at least as long as the loan term. Confirm the current version with your lender. Four: key contracts. What carries over, and what ends with the seller? Five: inventory, plus zoning and environmental matters. Bring in an attorney and a CPA for this. Save this before your next offer.

fact_refs.claim: In SBA change-of-ownership deals, lenders review the seller's financial information and, under SOP 50 10 8, verify it against IRS tax transcripts.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying an existing business] Hypothetical scenario: two partners, one wants out. A partner buyout can be financed as a partial change of ownership

scripts.problem: Owners don't realize a partner buyout can be a financed change of ownership with its own valuation and equity considerations, so they improvise funding or delay the exit.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amounts used. Hypothetical fifty-fifty ownership split only. The provisional ~USD 300,000 figure is not mentioned.
scripts.hook: Your business partner wants out. Buying their share? That's an acquisition too.
scripts.script: Your business partner wants out. Buying their share? That's an acquisition too. Here's a hypothetical. Two partners own a business fifty-fifty. One wants to retire. The other wants to stay and buy that half. Instead of draining the company's cash, the staying partner looks at financing. As of October twenty twenty-six, the SBA lists complete or partial changes of ownership as eligible uses of seven-A loans. That's an SBA-guaranteed loan made by a lender. Rules can change, and every deal still needs lender approval. But here's the first big question, and it's not the rate. What is the business actually worth? Under the current SBA rules, every change of ownership reportedly needs an independent business valuation. And equity requirements in a partial buyout can differ from a full purchase. Your attorney handles the partnership agreement side. Facing a partner buyout in the next year? Send us a DM.
scripts.cta: Facing a partner buyout in the next year? Send us a DM.
scripts.recording_notes_es: Plano medio-cerrado, tono de conversación cercana, como contando una situación. Decir 'Here's a hypothetical' con claridad y una pausa. 7(a) loans are made by lenders with a partial SBA guaranty.

Equity injection requirements for partial changes of ownership can differ from complete changes of ownership (no percentage stated).
Two partners, fifty-fifty ownership, one retiring: hypothetical illustration.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying an existing business] Question: what happens to the seller's existing liabilities and the lease when you buy a business (asset vs. stock purchase; lease term)
scripts.audience: First-time acquisition buyers early in deal evaluation
scripts.problem: Buyers don't understand how existing liabilities and the premises lease carry over; a short lease can derail financing late in the process.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amounts used. The provisional ~USD 300,000 figure is not mentioned.
scripts.hook: The seller still owes money on the business. Does that become your problem?
scripts.script: The seller still owes money on the business. Does that become your problem? It depends on the deal structure. In an asset purchase, you buy the business's assets, not the legal company. Generally, you don't take on the seller's liabilities. In a stock purchase, you buy the company, and generally its liabilities come with it. Exceptions exist, so talk to your attorney and CPA. Now the part that's easy to check too late: the lease. Under SBA rules, as of October twenty twenty-six and subject to change, the lease term, including renewal options only the business can exercise, generally needs to run at least as long as the loan term. Confirm the current version with your lender. Read the lease early. How much time is left, and how does it transfer to you? Questions about an acquisition? Send us a DM.

fact_refs.claim: Generally, an asset buyer does not take on the seller's liabilities, while a stock buyer takes the whole company, liabilities included; exceptions exist.

Under SOP 50 10 8, the lease term including renewal options exercisable solely by the business must be at least equal to the loan term (as of Oct 2026, subject to change; 8.1 status to confirm with lender).

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying an existing business] Myth vs. reality: 'An earn-out is basically the same as a seller note.' What an earn-out is and how it's reportedly treated in SBA 7(a) acquisitions
scripts.audience: Acquisition buyers negotiating price gaps with sellers
scripts.problem: Buyers propose earn-outs to bridge valuation gaps without knowing SBA financing may not allow contingent price structures, which can force a late restructure.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amounts used. The provisional ~USD 300,000 figure is not mentioned.
scripts.hook: "We'll just do an earn-out." In an SBA deal, that may not fly.
scripts.script: "We'll just do an earn-out." In an SBA deal, that may not fly. Here's the myth: an earn-out is basically the same as a seller note. Reality: they're different tools. An earn-out is a future payment to the seller that depends on how the business performs after closing. Hit the targets, the seller gets more. Miss them, the seller gets less. Here's why that matters. As of October twenty twenty-six, industry sources report that seller earn-outs aren't allowed in SBA seven-A acquisitions, because the purchase price can't be contingent. Seven-A is an SBA-guaranteed loan from a lender. A buyer rebate tied to performance after closing is reportedly allowed. These rules can change, so confirm with your lender and attorney before putting an earn-out in an offer. Know someone negotiating a business purchase? Send them this.
scripts.cta: Know someone negotiating a business purchase? Send them this.

Al decir 'myth' y 'reality' marcar el contraste con una pausa. En 'Hit the targets... Miss them' usar la mano subiendo y bajando. Cierre cálido mirando a cámara.
scripts.adaptation_note_es: De V12 (@owneractions) solo se adapta el mecanismo de una afirmación matizada con salvedades sobre financiación del vendedor. No se copian frases ni se repite la explicación de seller notes de ayer; aquí el seller note solo aparece como contraste.

fact_refs.claim: An earn-out is a contingent future payment to the seller that depends on how the business performs after closing.

Under SOP 50 10 8/8.1, seller earn-outs are reportedly not allowed in 7(a) change-of-ownership deals because the price can't be contingent; buyer rebates tied to post-close performance are reportedly allowed (exact SOP section not retrieved; as of Oct 2026, subject to change).
7(a) loans are made by lenders with a partial SBA guaranty.
